SELECT bm25(entries_fts, 2.0, 8.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0, 3.0) AS score,
       e.id, e.title, e.type, e.domain, e.subdomain, e.refutes,

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Explicit 52-card deck ordering: the four suits laid out in blocks, each block in ascending rank order — A(spades),2S,3S,...,KS, AH,2H,...,KH, AD,...,KD, AC,...,KC. This is a genuine permutation of the 52 distinct (rank,suit) cards (verified by the script: 52 cards, all distinct, sorted multiset equals the full deck). Brute-force checking each of the 47 windows of 6 consecutive positions shows 32 of them are straights (ranks ascending by exactly one): windows starting at positions 1-8, 14-21, 27-34, 40-47. So this single deck contains 32 length-6 straights, not at most 8. The script also proves 32 is exactly the true maximum: every maximal ascending-by-one run has length <= 13 (ranks live in 1..13), a length-6 window is a straight iff it lies inside one maximal run, so the count equals sum over runs of max(0, L_i - 5) with sum L_i = 52 and L_i <= 13; exhaustively enumerating all 148702 partitions of 52 into parts <= 13 maximises this at 32, attained by (13,13,13,13) — which the witness realises.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the inclusion-exclusion / overcounting discussion for player D's expected-count estimate, the answer asserts that the maximum number of 6-card straights that can appear in one shuffled 52-card deck is 8 (illustrated by eight pairwise-disjoint 6-card blocks). This bounds the overcount of the union-bound estimate 47 * (32/52)(4/51)(4/50)(4/49)(4/48)(4/47) = 1/9518. The true maximum number of straight-occurrences (windows of 6 consecutive positions whose ranks ascend by one) is 32, because straights may overlap.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> I think worst case there could be $8$ straights of length $6$ in the same deck but that would be an astronomically rare event.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Probability 2 player card game with multiple patterns to win, who has the advantage?
> 
> $2$ people (C and D) decide to play a computer assisted game.  The computer is programmed to quickly play as many fair hands (using the equivalent of a fair $52$ card deck), until someone wins the hand so the win will appear instantly when they press a button on the keyboard and then it waits for the next keypress for the next game. The computer is necessary because of how infrequent wins are, thus a real deck of cards would take way too long between wins.
> 
> The rules are player C can win if he gets $3$ "gapped" $3$ card straights dealt in order.  An A (ace) will be considered the highest rank for both C and D so $A23~567~9TJ$ (T = ten rank) would NOT be a win for C but $234~QKA~789$ would be. There has to be at least a gap of $1$ rank between the $3$ card straights but can be wider as shown in th [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a worst-case bound of 8 on the number of length-6 straights in one deck, used to bound the inclusion-exclusion overcount of the first-moment estimate 47*(32/52)(4/51)(4/50)(4/49)(4/48)(4/47) = 256/2436525 (= 1/9517.67..., the post's "1/9518"). The 47 events being union-bounded are the 47 windows of 6 consecutive positions, and these windows OVERLAP, so the relevant maximum is the number of straight-occurrences that can hold simultaneously, not the number of disjoint straights. The witness deck realises 32 of the 47 events at once, four times the claimed worst case; the exhaustive partition argument shows 32 is exactly the true maximum, so the assertion is off by a factor of 4 and the overcount bound built on it is wrong. Honest caveat recorded in the script output: under the alternative reading "pairwise DISJOINT straights", floor(52/6) = 8 is correct, so 8 is defensible only for that reading, which is not the quantity the inclusion-exclusion/overcount discussion requires. Method validation (negative control): for four small analogues (R ranks, 2 copies each, straight length k) the script enumerates EVERY distinct rank arrangement exhaustively (2520, 2520, 113400 and 7484400 arrangements), asserts the run-decomposition counting identity on each one, and confirms the brute-force maximum equals the partition bound in all four cases — so the bounding method used for the 52-card case is validated where full brute force is feasible. All arithmetic is exact ints; the probability uses fractions.Fraction only; the one float printed is an explicitly labelled echo used in no decision. Runtime ~21 s.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Let L={0,a,b,c,1}, ordered by 0<a,b,c<1 with a,b,c pairwise incomparable (the five-element diamond M₃). It is a complete lattice: finite joins and meets exist; distinct atoms join to 1 and meet to 0. But a ∧ (b ∨ c)=a ∧ 1=a, whereas (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c)=0 ∨ 0=0. Since a≠0, finite meet does not distribute over arbitrary join, so L is not a frame.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **Every complete lattice is an object of Frm, so CLat is a subcategory of Frm.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> From Complete Lattice Homomorphism is Frame Homomorphism:
> $\mathbf{CLat}$ consists of a subcollection of objects and subcollection of morphisms of $\mathbf{Frm}$

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Category CLat is Subcategory of Frm
> 
> Let $\mathbf{Frm}$ denote the category of frames.
> 
> Let $\mathbf{CLat}$ denote the category of complete lattices.
> 
> Then:
> $\mathbf{CLat}$ is a subcategory of $\mathbf{Frm}$

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

L satisfies the stated complete-lattice hypothesis but is not an object of Frm. Thus not every CLat object is a Frm object, and the asserted subcategory inclusion fails under the standard object definitions.

Verification notes from the pipeline:

> Exhaustive finite check validates M₃ as a complete lattice and exhibits failure of the frame distributivity axiom.
> Hypotheses independently checked: M₃ order is a poset; All 32 subsets of M₃ have unique joins and meets; a ∧ (b ∨ c) differs from (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c); Three-element chain is a complete lattice and a frame
> Claimed result: Every complete lattice is an object of Frm.
> Actual result: False: M₃ is complete but not a frame; lhs=a and rhs=0.
> Negative control: Passed: the three-element chain is a complete lattice and frame.
> Verifier correction: L={0,a,b,c,1} with 0 below three incomparable atoms a,b,c, all below 1.
> The independent Terra checker exited 0 and its stdout was cold-rerun and byte-matched by the verification audit.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Smallest witness: the directed 2-cycle C_2 with V = {v1, v2}, E = {v1->v2, v2->v1} (k = 2). Its transitive closure contains 4 reachable ordered pairs: v1~>v1, v1~>v2, v2~>v1, v2~>v2. Take the subset S of k-1 = 1 cycle edges S = {v2->v1}. S is indeed a spanning tree of the underlying undirected cycle (2 vertices, 1 edge, connected), exactly as the sentence describes. But the closure of (V, S) contains only 1 pair (v2~>v1). Claim says |TC(S)| = |TC(C)| = 4; here |TC(S)| = 1 != 4, with pairs v1~>v1, v1~>v2, v2~>v2 destroyed. The same failure occurs for the other subset {v1->v2}, and for every k in 2..12 and every one of the k subsets of size k-1: 77 of 77 tested (k-1)-subsets failed to preserve the transitive closure. Correspondingly, the number of transitive reductions of C_k (inclusion-minimal, and also minimum-cardinality, edge subsets with the same transitive closure) is exactly 1 for every k in 2..12 -- the whole cycle itself -- not k. This also refutes the drawn conclusion: the 2-cycle is cyclic yet has exactly one transitive reduction.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **Part 2's key step: that for a directed cycle C = v1→v2→…→vk→v1, any subset of k−1 of the cycle's edges "forms a spanning tree of C and suffices to maintain the reachability", yielding k distinct transitive reductions. This is false: deleting any single edge of a directed cycle destroys reachability pairs that are present in the transitive closure, so none of the claimed k reductions preserves G^T. (The same witness family also refutes the conclusion drawn from it: the 2-cycle has exactly one transitive reduction despite being cyclic.)**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> However, any subset of k −1 edges from C forms a spanning tree of C and suffices to maintain the reachability.

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 17
> Let G be a directed graph. Define the transitive closure GT as the directed graph sharing
> the same vertex set as G, where an edge u →v exists in GT if and only if there is a
> directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to be a
> graph with the minimum number of edges such that its transitive closure is identical to
> GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that
> G possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a finitely checkable statement: for a directed cycle C = v1->...->vk->v1, every (k-1)-subset of E(C) induces the same reachability relation as C. The script computes exact transitive closures with the boolean Warshall algorithm over integer bitmasks (no floats, no randomness, stdlib only) and finds this false for every k tested. Mechanism: in a directed cycle the closure is the complete relation on V (all k^2 ordered pairs, including self-reachability), because every vertex reaches every vertex by going around. Deleting any single edge (v_i -> v_{i+1}) leaves a directed path, whose closure is only the strict linear order along that path: k(k-1)/2 pairs instead of k^2. So all k^2 - k(k-1)/2 remaining pairs (including all self-loops v~>v and every "backwards" pair) are lost. The proof's error is conflating an undirected spanning-tree/connectivity argument with directed reachability: a (k-1)-edge subset does span C as an undirected tree, but directed reachability is not preserved. Consequently the claimed k distinct transitive reductions do not exist; a directed cycle has a unique transitive reduction (itself). Negative control: an exhaustive sweep over ALL 4164 digraphs on n <= 4 labeled vertices shows that a cycle edge can be deletable without changing the closure only when extra edges outside the cycle supply the redundancy (15552 such deletions at n=4, 36 at n=3), never for the bare cycle itself (0 at n=2 where the only cyclic graph is C_2); so the stated justification is unsound as written even though some cyclic graphs do have several transitive reductions (max 58 among 4-vertex digraphs) for entirely different reasons.

## Remarks

- Provenance: record `Algorithms_17__sol5`, corpus "QEDBench, second-model flags (confirmed)" of the proof-verification canonical-600 confirmed set (commit e33026ae); full dossier in that repository's `iclr_submission/supplement_dossiers.pdf`.
- Verification: zero-import Lean 4 certificate vendored at `lean/canonical600/Algorithms_17__sol5.lean` (kernel-checked in the source pipeline; certificate route None).

On the unit circle about O=(0,0), let θ₁(t)=t, θ₂(t)=2t, θ₃(t)=π/2+(1+√2)t, with positions (cos θᵢ,sin θᵢ). These are three circular orbits with distinct positive constant speeds 1, 2, and 1+√2.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **Three or more bodies orbiting a single point at distinct constant speeds are guaranteed eventually to align.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Given a 2D system of 3 or more bodies that orbit a single point, is it guaranteed that they will all align at some point? Assume that each body orbits at a different, yet constant speeds

Context of the original problem:

> Would all planets be guaranteed to align at some point if they orbit in a 2D plane?

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

Central alignment requires θ₂−θ₁ and θ₃−θ₁ both lie in πℤ. The first condition gives t=kπ. The second would then require 1/2+k√2∈ℤ. For k=0 this is false; for k≠0 it would make √2 rational. Thus no t≥0 aligns them, contradicting the claimed guarantee. This also rules out same-ray alignment.

> The standalone checker encodes the angular laws exactly, proves the submitted three-orbit system has no central alignment for t>=0, and thus also no same-ray alignment.

> Negative control: Replacing the third speed with 5/2 gives central alignment at t=pi.
> Full-source semantic scope: The source literally asserts a universal eventual-alignment guarantee for three or more bodies with distinct constant orbital speeds. The verified three-body unit-circle witness has positive pairwise-distinct constant speeds and no central alignment at any real time, so it directly negates that claim without dropping a stated premise.

## Object

  Type A: n = 2 children, boy-probability p_A = 3/4, population weight 1/2
  Type B: n = 3 children, boy-probability p_B = 1/2, population weight 1/2

Recomputed quantities (exact Fractions; K = boys, N = family size):

  E[K]        = 1/2·2·(3/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 3/2
  E[#brothers | uniformly random MAN]   = (21/16)/(3/2) = 7/8   = 0.875
  E[K(N-K)]   = 1/2·2·1·(3/4)(1/4) + 1/2·3·2·(1/2)(1/2) = 15/16
  E[N-K]      = 1/2·2·(1/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 1
  E[#brothers | uniformly random WOMAN] = (15/16)/1     = 15/16 = 0.9375

So MAN (14/16) < WOMAN (15/16), deficit exactly 1/16 — the opposite of the asserted "men on average have more brothers". Both averages were independently re-derived by brute-force enumeration of all 2^n sex sequences of each family type with exact rational sequence probabilities, counting brothers person-by-person; the enumeration agrees exactly with the closed form (assertion in the script).

> 
> I think women have more as no man can be his own brother. But how one can prove it rigorously?
>

The flagged claim: **The load-bearing lemma: in any 2(k+1)-edge-connected graph G there is a spanning tree T with G/E(T) 2k-edge-connected, together with the supporting cut count ("the edges between A and B consist of exactly one edge e of T plus at most 2k-1 other edges ... at most 2k") and the lift step that turns k spanning trees of G/E(T) into k trees of G edge-disjoint from T.**

> Proof of lemma: We need to show that in any 2(k + 1)-edge-connected graph G, there exists a spanning tree T such that G/E(T) is 2k-edge-connected.

Context of the original problem:

> Problem Statement
> Problem: Algorithms - 38
> Suppose G is a 2k-edge-connected graph. Prove that there exist k pairwise edge-disjoint
> spanning trees in G.
> 1

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

Statement decided. "G/E(T)" cannot mean literal contraction of a spanning tree (that collapses G to one vertex and makes the lemma vacuous); the lift step quoted in the claim ("turn k spanning trees of G/E(T) into k trees of G edge-disjoint from T") forces the reading G/E(T) = G - E(T), the graph on the same vertex set with the n-1 tree edges deleted. So the load-bearing lemma is the finitely refutable statement LEMMA(k): every 2(k+1)-edge-connected graph G has a spanning tree T with lambda(G - E(T)) >= 2k. The witness refutes LEMMA(1), which is the base case the whole induction rests on.

Why it fails: the witness graph is 4-regular, so removing a spanning tree leaves every vertex with degree 4 - d_T(v); to keep min degree >= 2 the tree must have max degree <= 2, i.e. it must be a Hamiltonian path. But every Hamiltonian path of this graph either disconnects the remainder or leaves a bridge, because each of the 8 doubled edges that the path does NOT use survives with multiplicity 2, and both of its endpoints then have all their remaining degree inside that doubled pair unless they are path endpoints - only 2 vertices can be path endpoints, so at most one doubled edge can be missed, and the Moebius-Kantor graph has no Hamiltonian path using 7 or 8 of these alternating edges in a way that leaves a bridgeless remainder. Exhaustive enumeration confirms max_T lambda(G-E(T)) = 1 < 2.

The proof's supporting cut count is refuted directly and is in fact the source of the error. The proof argues that if (A,B) were a cut of G-E(T) with fewer than 2k edges, then "the edges between A and B consist of exactly one edge e of T plus at most 2k-1 other edges ... at most 2k", contradicting 2(k+1)-edge-connectivity. That step silently assumes a spanning tree crosses a cut exactly once. It does not: a spanning tree crosses (A,B) exactly comp(T[A]) + comp(T[B]) - 1 times, which can be arbitrarily large. In the witness, with T the Hamiltonian path 0-1-...-15 and A = {0,1,4,5,8,9,12,13}, the tree crosses the cut SEVEN times, so |delta_G(A)| = 8 rather than <= 2k = 2, no contradiction with 4-edge-connectivity is reached, and indeed delta_{G-E(T)}(A) has only 1 edge.

Getting a 2k-edge-connected remainder from tree packing alone would need (4k+2)-edge-connectivity, far more than the lemma assumes. (Consistently, the sweeps confirm the lemma is not universally false - it holds for all 588 4-regular simple graphs on <= 8 vertices, all 1580 4-edge-connected 4-regular multigraphs on <= 6 vertices, and 2841 further 4-regular graphs - it is simply not a theorem.)

Honest caveats: (i) the witness is a multigraph (two parallel edges on 8 pairs). Multigraphs are the standard setting for edge-connectivity and for the Nash-Williams/Tutte tree-packing theorem the proof is establishing, and the proof text imposes no simplicity hypothesis, so this refutes the lemma as stated; but a reader who insists on simple graphs would not be refuted by this witness. ## Object

Explicit 52-card deck ordering: the four suits laid out in blocks, each block in ascending rank order — A(spades),2S,3S,...,KS, AH,2H,...,KH, AD,...,KD, AC,...,KC. This is a genuine permutation of the 52 distinct (rank,suit) cards (verified by the script: 52 cards, all distinct, sorted multiset equals the full deck). Brute-force checking each of the 47 windows of 6 consecutive positions shows 32 of them are straights (ranks ascending by exactly one): windows starting at positions 1-8, 14-21, 27-34, 40-47. So this single deck contains 32 length-6 straights, not at most 8. The script also proves 32 is exactly the true maximum: every maximal ascending-by-one run has length <= 13 (ranks live in 1..13), a length-6 window is a straight iff it lies inside one maximal run, so the count equals sum over runs of max(0, L_i - 5) with sum L_i = 52 and L_i <= 13; exhaustively enumerating all 148702 partitions of 52 into parts <= 13 maximises this at 32, attained by (13,13,13,13) — which the witness realises.

## Object

Order on $\mathbb{R}\times_\ell \{0,1\}$: compare real parts first; ties broken by the
Boolean. The "double arrow"-style doubling makes each pair $\{(x,0),(x,1)\}$ an
adjacency: $((x,0),(x,1))$-type gaps force any basis to distinguish uncountably many
points, killing second countability; density of (ℚ-indexed) points survives.

## What it kills

The silent metric-space reflex "separable, so take a countable basis" — one of the
most common gaps when general-topological arguments are transplanted from analysis.
(Its second-countable ⇒ hereditarily separable cousin fails elsewhere too.)

## Debugging uses

- Audit any proof that builds a countable object (basis, partition of unity index,
  Borel hierarchy argument) from separability alone.
- Measure-theoretic relevance: standard Borel space machinery needs second countable,
  not merely separable — this is where "Polish space" hypotheses in descriptive set
  theory and probability come from and why they can't be weakened casually.

## References

Mathlib: `RealProdLexBool.not_secondCountableTopology` (Counterexamples library).
Cousin of the double arrow space in Steen & Seebach (unverified citation).

## Object

For conditionally convergent $\sum a_n$: the positive terms alone sum to $+\infty$, the
negative to $-\infty$, and $a_n \to 0$. Greedy algorithm for target $s$: take positive
terms until the partial sum exceeds $s$, then negative until below, repeat. Overshoot at
each reversal is at most the last term used $\to 0$, so the rearrangement converges to $s$.

## What it kills

Silent reindexing/reordering of infinite sums. "Since addition is commutative..." is
valid for finitely many terms only; for infinite sums it needs absolute convergence.

## Debugging uses

- Audit any proof that reorders a series, sums over an index set "in a different order",
  swaps a double sum, or groups terms — each such step needs absolute convergence
  (Fubini–Tonelli for sums) or an explicit argument.
- Floating-point/parallel computing: reduction order changes results for near-cancelling
  sums; this is the exact-arithmetic limit of that phenomenon. Deterministic reductions
  and compensated summation exist precisely because of it.
- The greedy proof itself is an algorithm — useful as a generator of adversarial
  orderings when testing summation code.

## Remarks

Grouping (inserting parentheses) is safe for convergent series, but *removing*
parentheses is not: Σ(1−1) = 0 while 1−1+1−1+... diverges.
hits.counterexample: If Σ a_n converges conditionally (converges, but Σ|a_n| = ∞), then for every s ∈ [−∞, +∞] there is a rearrangement summing to s, and rearrangements can also be made to oscillate. Example: the alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − ... = ln 2, but rearranged to take two positive terms per negative term it sums to (3/2)ln 2.
hits.refutes: Addition being commutative, the sum of a convergent series does not depend on the order of its terms.

hits.counterexample: Explicit 52-card deck ordering: the four suits laid out in blocks, each block in ascending rank order — A(spades),2S,3S,...,KS, AH,2H,...,KH, AD,...,KD, AC,...,KC. This is a genuine permutation of the 52 distinct (rank,suit) cards (verified by the script: 52 cards, all distinct, sorted multiset equals the full deck). Brute-force checking each of the 47 windows of 6 consecutive positions shows 32 of them are straights (ranks ascending by exactly one): windows starting at positions 1-8, 14-21, 27-34, 40-47. So this single deck contains 32 length-6 straights, not at most 8. The script also proves 32 is exactly the true maximum: every maximal ascending-by-one run has length <= 13 (ranks live in 1..13), a length-6 window is a straight iff it lies inside one maximal run, so the count equals sum over runs of max(0, L_i - 5) with sum L_i = 52 and L_i <= 13; exhaustively enumerating all 148702 partitions of 52 into parts <= 13 maximises this at 32, attained by (13,13,13,13) — which the witness realises. The negation of the quoted claim on this witness is machine-checked by a self-contained (zero-import) Lean 4 kernel certificate.
hits.refutes: In the inclusion-exclusion / overcounting discussion for player D's expected-count estimate, the answer asserts that the maximum number of 6-card straights that can appear in one shuffled 52-card deck is 8 (illustrated by eight pairwise-disjoint 6-card blocks). This bounds the overcount of the union-bound estimate 47 * (32/52)(4/51)(4/50)(4/49)(4/48)(4/47) = 1/9518. The true maximum number of straight-occurrences (windows of 6 consecutive positions whose ranks ascend by one) is 32, because straights may overlap.
